blocks.text: Chapter 34. Attaining the Way by the Middle Course

inline.s: A renunciant was reciting at night the Bequeathed Teachings of the Buddha Kashyapa, his voice mournful and strained, and he began to think of retreating from the path. The Buddha asked him: When you dwelt at home, what was your occupation? He replied: I loved to play the lute. The Buddha asked: If the strings are too loose, how is it? He replied: They give forth no sound. The Buddha asked: If too taut? He replied: The note breaks off. The Buddha asked: If, neither loose nor taut, the strings are tuned aright? He replied: Then all the notes are harmonious. The Buddha said: Even so is the renunciant who studies the Way — if the mind is tuned aright, the Way is attained. If one is violent in the Way, violence wearies the body; when the body is weary, the mind grows vexed; when the mind is vexed, the practice recedes; and when the practice recedes, guilt increases all the more. Only in purity and serene ease is the Way not lost.

A renunciant recited at night the Bequeathed Teachings of the Buddha Kashyapa, his voice mournful and strained, feeling that the study of the Way was too hard and too wearying, and wishing to give up. The Buddha asked him: When you were at home, what was your trade? He answered: I loved to play the lute; playing the lute was my trade. The Buddha asked: If the strings are loosened too far, what happens? He answered: No note comes forth. The Buddha asked: If they are drawn too tight? He answered: They snap at a touch. The Buddha asked: If they are tuned just right, loose and tight in measure? He answered: Every note is true and sweet. The Buddha then taught: Studying the Way is like this — if body and mind are tuned aright, in just proportion, then as you practice you may attain the Way. If you are too fierce and urgent, then a person grows weary; weary, the mind grows vexed; vexed, you think of retreating and giving up; and once you give up, guilt and evil accumulate until you fall. Only by tuning body and mind aright, in purity and ease, can you advance steadily, practice long and with effect, and so never turn back.
[Buddha Kashyapa] The Buddha who came before Shakyamuni Buddha.

Confucius, too, had a word on tension and relaxation, saying: “To be always strained and never relaxed — even Kings Wen and Wu of the Zhou could not sustain it; to be always relaxed and never strained — that is something Kings Wen and Wu would never do. Let tension and relaxation alternate, and that is the way of Wen and Wu.”

This passage means: to keep straining without ever relaxing is beyond the power even of King Wen and King Wu, who governed the realm so well; and conversely, to remain forever at ease without ever straining is something Wen and Wu would never consent to. Only by joining labor and rest, severity and leniency, so that work and life move forward in their proper rhythm — this is how King Wen and King Wu governed the land.
Therefore the practice of the Way should be continuous and unbroken — water dripping slowly wears through stone.

blocks.text: Chapter 35. When the Defilements Are Cleansed, the Brightness Remains

inline.s: The Buddha said: Just as a man forges iron and, casting off the dross, makes a vessel, so the vessel at last proves fine and excellent — in the same way one who studies the Way, by removing the defilements of the heart, becomes pure in conduct.

Just as by forging iron into a vessel — hammering out the dross within — the vessel becomes fine and durable, so the student of the Way, by removing the defilements of the heart, becomes pure in conduct.
Therefore, practice is the cultivating of the mind: remove the heart’s defilements.

[Just as a man forges iron, casting off dross to make a vessel] Today steelmaking removes the impurities from molten iron by chemical means to obtain steel, which is then forged into tools. In ancient times the iron was heated red-hot and hammered again and again, each time driving out the dross, until steel was won — the proverb “a hundred refinements make steel.” For tools and weapons, steel is far sharper and more lasting than iron. Hence in olden days, to forge a vessel meant not only beating it into the desired shape but, in the very process, casting out the dross within — what is called “casting off the dross to make a vessel.”

blocks.text: Chapter 36. Winning the Goal Through Every Hardship

inline.s: The Buddha said: Having escaped the evil destinies, it is hard to be born a human. Becoming a human, it is hard to be born a man and not a woman. Being born a man, it is hard to be born with the six faculties whole. With the six faculties whole, it is hard to be born in the central kingdom. Born in the central kingdom, it is hard to meet a Buddha in the world. Meeting a Buddha, it is hard to encounter one who walks the Way. Encountering such a one, it is hard to arouse a heart of faith. Having aroused faith, it is hard to set forth the bodhi mind. Having set forth the bodhi mind, it is hard to be without practice and without attainment.

It is hard, having left the three evil destinies, to be born a human. Born a human, it is hard to be a man and not a woman. Born a man, it is hard to have the six faculties whole. Having the six faculties, it is hard to be born in the central kingdom. Born in the central kingdom, it is hard to meet a Buddha alive in the world. Meeting a Buddha, it is hard to encounter the Dharma. Encountering the Dharma, it is hard to arouse a heart of faith. Having aroused faith, it is hard to develop the aspiration to enlightenment. Having developed the bodhisattva resolve (the bodhi mind), it is hard to be without practice and without attainment.

[Three evil destinies] The hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, the animal world. [Six faculties whole] The six faculties are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. To be whole in the six faculties means to lack the defects of blindness, deafness, dumbness, and maimed limbs. [Central kingdom] The “central kingdom” of ancient India, lying in the middle reaches of the Ganges, the heart of its civilization. [Bodhi mind] The resolve to attain Buddhahood above and deliver sentient beings below. [Without practice and without attainment] What was described earlier: the one ultimate vehicle, the most consummate path. [One vehicle] The way to Buddhahood.

This chapter means: good conditions are met by the student of the Way only after a hundred hardships and a thousand trials; and now, having struggled through to the step of setting forth the bodhisattva resolve, he should cultivate the most ultimate path.

blocks.text: Chapter 37. Keeping the Precepts Draws One Near the Way

inline.s: The Buddha said: Though a disciple be thousands of miles from me, if he keeps my precepts in mind, he shall surely attain the fruit of the Way. One who stands at my side, though he see me every day, if he does not follow my precepts, shall never attain the Way.

Though a disciple of the Buddha be thousands of miles from me, if he bears my precepts in mind, he shall surely attain the fruit of the Way. One who is at my side, though he sees me constantly, if he does not keep my precepts, shall never attain the Way.

Even to wait upon the Buddha on his left and right, without strictly keeping the precepts, one still cannot attain the Way — how much the more so in this latter age of the Dharma. From this we may know how essential it is to observe the precepts with strict severity.

The Buddha asked a renunciant: In how many intervals does a human life consist? He answered: Within a few days. The Buddha said: You do not yet know the Way. He asked another renunciant: In how many intervals does a human life consist? He answered: Within the space of a single meal. The Buddha said: You do not yet know the Way. He asked a third: In how many intervals does a human life consist? He answered: Within a single breath. The Buddha praised him: Well said — now you know the Way!

The Buddha asked one renunciant: In how many intervals does a human life consist? He answered: Within a few days. The Buddha said: You have not yet understood the Way. He asked another: In how many intervals does a human life consist? He answered: Within the space of one meal. The Buddha said: You have not yet understood the Way. He asked yet another: In how many intervals does a human life consist? He answered: Within one breath. The Buddha praised him: Excellent — now you understand the Way!
[Within a single breath] In the space of one in-and-out breath life may come to an end — what is meant by “the out-breath does not guarantee the in-breath.”

This chapter makes it clear: human life is impermanent, the out-breath does not guarantee the in-breath, and so the student of the Way must be alert and diligent, completing his task before death arrives.

blocks.text: Chapter 39. Sweet in the Midst and Sweet at the Edge

inline.s: The Buddha said: Those who study the Buddha’s Way should believe and follow all that the Buddha has spoken. It is like tasting honey — sweet in the midst and sweet at the edge; such likewise are my scriptures.

One who studies the Buddha’s Way should believe and follow everything the Buddha has spoken. As with the taste of honey, sweet at the heart and sweet at the rim, so too are the scriptures I have spoken.

Here the Buddha admonishes with heartfelt earnestness: those who study the Buddha’s Way should believe and follow all the Buddha’s words. Now there are those who, clinging to the small (the Hinayana), slander the great (the Mahayana), or clinging to the great, slander the small; those who cling to phenomena and reject principle, or cling to principle and reject phenomena — all of these run against the Buddha’s intent.

It is like studying mathematics. Someone judges arithmetic too elementary and would go straight to algebra; another finds algebra not lofty enough and would leap straight to calculus. And what is the result? After great effort they memorize a handful of terms and formulas from algebra or calculus and grow pleased with themselves, saying “I know algebra, I know calculus.” But can they solve a single problem with it? Since they cannot, of what use is their learning?

Studying the Buddha’s Dharma means subduing afflictions, severing afflictions, breaking through ignorance piece by piece, and realizing the fruit of Buddhahood in its fullness, so as to be done with the two deaths (the death born of segments and the death born of transformation). The Buddha’s teachings are set down for this very end. “Medicine is neither dear nor common; what suits the ailment is good. The Dharma is neither high nor low; what suits the capacity is excellent.” Therefore the student of the Way must take the medicine that suits his ailment, and learn so as to put it to use. If your own afflictions are not yet subdued, not yet cut off, and yet you scoff at the Buddha’s repeated admonition to “sever desire and cast off attachment” as mere Hinayana, refusing even to consider it, while you prattle on about the nature and the principle — is this not like one who, never having studied arithmetic or algebra, would go straight to calculus? When the last day of the twelfth month — the day of reckoning — arrives, will such learning stand you in good stead?

[Death born of segments] Among sentient beings within the three realms and six paths, because of the retribution of good and evil karma, the lifespan has its fixed limits and the body its divisions; hence their birth and death is called “death born of segments.” One who is done with this death is freed from the wheel of rebirth and passes beyond the three realms. [Death born of transformation] The noble ones of the three vehicles, having already severed the delusions of views and of thought and passed beyond the death of segments, find in the course of practice that delusive thoughts gradually die away and realization gradually grows. This shifting of delusion and awakening differs at each stage; the passage from one stage into the next is like a death, and the change is subtle, mysterious, and inconceivable — whence the name “death born of transformation.” One who is done with this realizes the fruit of Buddhahood in its fullness. [Three vehicles] The vehicle of the Hearer (Shravaka), the vehicle of the Solitary Realizer (Pratyekabuddha), and the vehicle of the Bodhisattva.
